description: We aim to make exploring the universe more accessible through an interactive tool built around NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Our project will let users explore the sky across infrared wavelengths, visualize astronomical observations, and investigate celestial objects. By transforming complex scientific data into interactive visualizations, we hope to inspire curiosity and make space science easier to understand.
summary:
We developed a web tool for exploring SPHEREx observations by sky position. Users enter Right Ascension and declination to search the archive, then view processed image cutouts on an interactive sky map. The tool can load observations from different dates, display them in a time slider, and provide FITS files for further analysis. It also looks for previously prepared images so cached examples can load quickly for demonstrations.

This addresses the challenge by making it easier for the public to compare infrared observations of the same patch of sky over time and spot possible changes or moving objects. The interactive map provides spatial context, while the dated images help users see how a field evolves. The tool supports exploration and discovery; scientific interpretation still requires reviewing the underlying measurements and observation metadata.
details:
What it does and how it works

The SPHEREx Sky Explorer lets users enter a sky position using Right Ascension and declination, then searches the SPHEREx archive through the project’s backend. Users can load observations of that region, view processed image cutouts on an interactive sky map, and move through prepared images in date order with a time slider. The app checks for previously prepared images so cached examples can load quickly; when an image is not yet prepared, it can be downloaded and processed through the backend.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes time-based sky exploration more approachable for the public. Comparing images from different dates can help users notice changing sources or possible moving objects and identify regions that may merit further study. It is an exploration tool, rather than an automatic discovery or confirmation system: users should assess candidate changes using the underlying data and observation context.

Tools and development

The frontend is built with React and TypeScript, with CSS for the interface and an interactive canvas sky map. It communicates with a Python backend that provides archive searches, image downloads, cutout processing, and stored product access. The backend uses NASA/IPAC IRSA services for SPHEREx archive data, and Docker Compose supports running the application’s services together. We also used AI tools, including ChatGPT and Claude, to help write and refine the frontend and backend code, research SPHEREx data, and explore scientific methods for validating the data and interpreting changes between observations. Our team reviewed and adapted the AI-assisted work to fit the project’s goals.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines a familiar coordinate search with a visual map and time slider, turning separate dated observations into a browsable sequence. We considered ease of use, clear observation dates, practical loading time through caching, and the distinction between display images and scientific measurements. The map’s starfield is decorative; the displayed observation cutouts come from the backend.
